THE FAMILY OF MATERIALS._summary: Materials are divided into metals and non-metals. Historically, civilizations were classified by their ability to work with metals. Modern materials include a wide variety such as ceramics, plastics, glass, and composites. Metals must compete in the market through superior performance and are categorized into ferrous (iron-based) and non-ferrous (non-iron-based) metals. Among non-ferrous metals, aluminum and copper alloys are widely used; ferrous metals include cast iron and steel, with steel classified by alloying elements. Steel designation systems are diverse, including AISI, ASTM, UNS, German Werkstoff, DIN, ISO, and Euronorm. Standards vary by country but are gradually moving toward unification.

Martensitic stainless steels are hardened by austenitizing, quenching, and tempering, with austenitizing temperatures typically ranging from 980 to 1010°C. Quenched hardness increases with temperature up to about 980°C, then decreases due to retained austenite. High-carbon types and complex sections require preheating at 790°C to prevent cracking. Due to high alloy content, air cooling is usually sufficient to achieve full hardness, but oil quenching is sometimes used for large sections. Tempering should be performed as soon as possible after quenching to avoid delayed cracking; for parts requiring high dimensional stability, cooling to -75°C before tempering can transform retained austenite. After tempering above 510°C, rapid cooling to below 400°C is necessary to avoid 475°C embrittlement.

Pitting corrosion._summary: This text describes localized pitting corrosion in stainless steel under conditions of chlorides, high temperature, and low pH, which can lead to pipe perforation. Pitting resistance is related to chromium, molybdenum, and nitrogen content, and can be evaluated using the PRE value (%Cr + 3.3 × %Mo + 16 × %N). The ASTM G48A test is used to determine the critical pitting temperature. In marine environments, 316 stainless steel may not fully resist pitting or tea staining; finer surface finishes (Ra ≤ 0.5 μm) help reduce tea staining. Alloys with higher chromium, molybdenum, and nitrogen content offer better pitting resistance.

Stress corrosion cracking (SCC)._summary: This text discusses stress corrosion cracking (SCC), a rapid and severe form of corrosion that occurs in stainless steel under the combined action of stress and a corrosive environment. The stress must be tensile, which can come from service loads, assembly stresses, or residual stresses from cold working. The most harmful environments are chloride-containing aqueous solutions (e.g., seawater), especially at high temperatures. Austenitic stainless steels (such as 304 and 316) are susceptible to this, with 316 being no more resistant than 304; duplex stainless steels (e.g., 2205) are almost immune below 150°C, super duplex stainless steels are even better, and ferritic stainless steels are generally unaffected. Improvement methods include introducing compressive stress through shot peening or eliminating tensile stress via final annealing, but careful evaluation is required. In practice, 304 can be used in water containing 100-300 ppm chlorides at moderate temperatures, but wet-dry conditions can concentrate chlorides, increasing the risk. Seawater contains about 2% chlorides and is used in heat exchangers above 50°C. Recent cases of chloride stress corrosion failure have been found at low temperatures (30-40°C), such as with 316 stainless steel fasteners above indoor chlorinated swimming pools, as well as failures at high temperatures with as little as 10 ppm chlorides; the issue is not yet fully understood.

Intergranular corrosion._summary: Intergranular corrosion is a rapid, localized form of corrosion associated with carbide precipitation. When austenitic steels are exposed to or slowly cooled within the temperature range of 425-850°C, chromium and carbon form chromium carbides along grain boundaries, depleting the adjacent areas of chromium and reducing corrosion resistance—a phenomenon known as sensitization. Carbon content, temperature, and time influence precipitation, with the most sensitive temperature being approximately 700°C. This condition can be remedied by heating above 1000°C followed by water quenching, or avoided by using stabilized grades (321, 347) or extra-low carbon steels (304L, 316L). Certain environments (e.g., room-temperature glacial acetic acid, alkaline solutions, fresh water) do not cause intergranular corrosion, and thin sheets are generally unaffected due to rapid cooling. Grain boundary carbides do not harm high-temperature strength, and high-carbon H-grade steels (e.g., 304H) are used for high-temperature applications. Sensitized steels may also be susceptible to intergranular stress corrosion cracking (IGSCC), though this is relatively rare.

Galvanic corrosion._summary: Galvanic corrosion is an electrochemical process caused by contact between dissimilar metals in an electrolyte. Three conditions are required: metals must be widely separated on the galvanic series, be in electrical contact, and have surfaces bridged by a conductive fluid. Prevention includes avoiding mixed metals, using insulating materials, or removing the electrolyte. The relative surface areas of the metals also affect corrosion rate; a large anodic area reduces corrosion, while a large cathodic area accelerates it. Examples include zinc-plated steel fasteners in stainless steel.

Contact corrosion._summary: This content discusses galvanic corrosion caused by contamination of stainless steel surfaces with carbon steel particles, including its mechanism (carbon steel particles act as an anode and corrode, potentially causing pitting of stainless steel), common causes (grinding of nearby carbon steel or tool contamination), and preventive measures (avoiding mixed metals, using insulating gaskets, improving drainage, protecting storage equipment, etc.). It also introduces methods for detecting contamination (rust test, copper sulfate test, 24-hour wet observation) and methods for removing contamination (passivation or pickling).

CORROSION RESISTANCE._summary: Corrosion resistance covers general, pitting, crevice, SCC, SSC, intergranular, galvanic, and contact corrosion.

Scaling Resistance

Creep Strength._summary: This article discusses the performance of different types of stainless steel at high temperatures. Austenitic stainless steels (such as 304H, 316L) have excellent creep strength and are suitable for high-temperature structural applications, while low-carbon versions (304L, 316L) have lower high-temperature strength. The oxidation resistance of ferritic stainless steels (such as 409, 430, 446) increases with chromium content, but their creep strength is lower than that of austenitic steels, making them commonly used in low-stress high-temperature environments. Duplex stainless steels are limited to use below 350°C due to high-temperature embrittlement. Martensitic and precipitation-hardening stainless steels are rarely used in high-temperature applications due to softening after heat treatment.

Structural Stability._summary: Discusses the issues of grain boundary carbide precipitation and sigma phase formation in stainless steel at high temperatures. Grain boundary carbides reduce corrosion resistance at 425-815°C, and stabilized or low-carbon grades are recommended. Sigma phase embrittles steel during prolonged exposure at 590-870°C, with high chromium, molybdenum, and silicon grades being susceptible, such as 310, 316, 317, and 314 grades. Grade 314 has been replaced due to severe embrittlement. Grade 310 is also unsuitable in this temperature range, and Grade 321 is often a better choice.

Thermal Expansion._summary: This text discusses the importance of thermal expansion of materials in high-temperature applications. The coefficient of thermal expansion is expressed as the proportional change in length per degree Celsius, with units such as ×10⁻⁶/°C or μm/m/°C. The expansion amount can be calculated by multiplying the original size by the temperature change and then by the coefficient. For example, a 3-meter-long 304 stainless steel rod heated from 20°C to 200°C will increase in length by 9.3 mm. The thermal expansion coefficient of austenitic stainless steel is higher than that of most other steel types and increases with temperature. Thermal expansion can cause bending or warping when components are constrained, especially when two different metals are connected and heated. The high expansion rate of austenitic stainless steel may lead to more dimensional issues than carbon steel or low-alloy steel. Non-austenitic stainless steel has higher thermal conductivity. Local stresses during heating and cooling can lead to stress corrosion cracking. Expansion joints should be used in design, and notches and abrupt cross-section changes should be avoided.

HIGH TEMPERATURE RESISTANCE._summary: High temperature resistance depends on scaling, creep, structural stability, environmental factors, and thermal expansion.

CRYOGENIC PROPERTIES._summary: Austenitic stainless steel has a unique combination of properties at cryogenic temperatures, with tensile strength significantly higher than at room temperature and only a slight decrease in toughness, making it suitable for cryogenic environments such as liquefied natural gas (-161°C), liquid oxygen (-183°C), and liquid nitrogen (-196°C). Its high coefficient of thermal expansion may lead to dimensional issues. Ferritic, martensitic, and precipitation-hardening stainless steels exhibit a significant decrease in toughness at cryogenic temperatures and are not recommended. Duplex stainless steel can be used above -50°C, but its toughness decreases below this temperature. Carbon steel and low-alloy steel also have a ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT), and these limitations are incorporated into design codes (e.g., AS1210). The ductile-to-brittle transition is reversible; steel that becomes brittle at low temperatures regains toughness upon warming.

MAGNETIC PROPERTIES._summary: This article mainly discusses the magnetic permeability characteristics of stainless steel. Austenitic stainless steel is almost non-magnetic in the annealed state, but cold working (such as wire drawing, rolling, and polishing) can induce martensite formation, leading to enhanced magnetic response. This is more pronounced in grades 304 and 303, while grades 310 and 316, due to their higher nickel-to-chromium ratio and more stable austenitic structure, exhibit a weaker magnetic response. The non-magnetic state can be restored through stress relief (heating at approximately 700-800°C) or solution treatment (1000-1150°C). Duplex stainless steel has better low-temperature toughness than ferritic and martensitic grades, but it has a ductile-to-brittle transition temperature. Castings and welds often contain 5-12% ferrite to prevent hot cracking, which can be measured using a ferrite meter. If magnetic permeability is a design factor, it must be specified at the time of procurement. Additionally, magnetically soft stainless steels (such as grade 18/2) are introduced for corrosion-resistant applications requiring rapid magnetic response, such as solenoid valves.

Mechanical Properties of Wire._summary: This article introduces the mechanical properties of stainless steel wire and bar, primarily described through tensile strength. Wires for different applications require carefully selected mechanical properties to enable forming during manufacturing and to withstand service loads. Spring wire has the highest tensile strength, making it suitable for coiling into springs; while braiding wire requires an appropriate balance of strength and flexibility for crimping and forming. Cold heading wire is used for fasteners, such as roofing bolts and self-tapping screws, requiring good ductility to form complex heads while being hard enough to prevent thread deformation, which necessitates careful consideration of steel composition to control the work hardening rate.

Mechanical Properties of Bar._summary: This article discusses two main manufacturing processes for austenitic stainless steel round bars: cold drawing (BD) for bars with diameters approximately 5mm to 26mm, which increases strength and yield stress through an area reduction of about 10%; and bars with diameters of approximately 26mm and above, which are made by hot rolling, annealing, and then turning (ST), with properties close to the annealed state. ST bars offer better machinability due to lower hardness and have a defect-free surface; BD bars may have minor surface imperfections. Cold working results in higher surface hardness than the core, while ST bars also exhibit surface hardening due to final machining and straightening. Figure 17 shows typical mechanical properties.

MECHANICAL PROPERTIES._summary: This article covers the mechanical properties of stainless steel wire and bar, including manufacturing processes.

Forming Operations._summary: This article mainly introduces the cold working characteristics of stainless steel, especially austenitic stainless steel. Austenitic stainless steel has high strength and an extremely high work hardening rate, so cold working requires greater force than carbon steel, and springback must be considered. Despite the high work hardening rate, its high ductility allows for deep cold forming, such as in the manufacture of kitchen sinks. Work hardening is the only way to harden austenitic stainless steel, while martensitic stainless steel can be hardened by quenching and tempering heat treatment. Although ferritic stainless steel can only be hardened by cold working, its hardening rate is low. Cold working can significantly increase strength; for example, 301, 302, and 304 stainless steel can achieve tensile strengths exceeding 2000 MPa after cold drawing, but this is limited to fine wires and small cross-sections. Large cross-sections are difficult to process uniformly due to rapid surface hardening. The work hardening rate decreases with increasing temperature, making deformation easier at low temperatures. Additionally, stainless steel deforms more severely during slow forming, unlike carbon steel. The work hardening rates of ferritic and martensitic stainless steels are similar to those of low-carbon steel, and they are magnetic. Martensitic stainless steel is typically heat-treated to obtain its properties, with cold working being more of a sizing operation.

Rules for Machining Stainless Steels._summary: General rules for machining austenitic stainless steel include: the machine tool must be rigid and free from vibration; cutting edges must be kept sharp, as dull tools cause surface work hardening; light but sufficiently deep cuts should be used to avoid tool sliding on the surface; all clearances should be adequate to prevent friction; tools should be as large as possible to dissipate heat; use chip breakers; maintain constant feed; use ample coolant and lubricant, as stainless steel has low thermal conductivity and heat concentrates at the cutting edge.

Brazing (\"Silver Soldering\")._summary: This article introduces the brazing method for stainless steel, which is suitable when welding is not feasible and a stronger joint than soft soldering is required. Brazing can be used to join non-ferrous metals such as copper, bronze, and nickel to stainless steel. The corrosion resistance of the joint is slightly lower than that of stainless steel, but it can meet requirements under normal temperature and mildly corrosive conditions. Since brazing temperatures may cause carbide precipitation (sensitization) in austenitic stainless steel, it is recommended to use low-carbon or stabilized grades (304L, 316L, 321). Ferritic grades (such as 430) can be quenched from brazing temperature, but martensitic grades (410, 420, 431) should not be heated above 760°C. Free-machining grades (303, 416, 430F) are generally not recommended due to the formation of dark slag on the surface. Recommended steps include: using silver brazing filler metal with a melting point of 590-870°C, cleaning the surface and immediately applying flux, heating uniformly with a slightly reducing flame, and using induction heating or controlled atmosphere furnaces for batch production. After brazing, remove residual flux. When brazing grade 430, it is recommended to use silver solder containing 3% nickel. Additionally, a general recommendation table for welding stainless steel is provided, covering precautions such as preheating, post-weld heat treatment, and filler metal selection.

Stress Relieving._summary: For austenitic stainless steel, stress relief is limited below 400°C; 425-925°C can significantly reduce residual stress (e.g., 870°C for one hour eliminates about 85%), but may cause grain boundary carbide precipitation and sensitization, impairing corrosion resistance. Stabilized or low-carbon grades (321, 304L, 316L) are recommended. Full annealing (approximately 1080°C with rapid cooling) can eliminate all stress but is not suitable for large or complex components. After cold working strengthening, treatment at 345-400°C for two hours can increase yield strength, commonly used for spring wire. Welded parts can be stress relieved below annealing temperature, especially suitable for large or dissimilar metal welds. Stress relief for martensitic or ferritic stainless steel welds can simultaneously temper and partially restore corrosion resistance, typically using subcritical annealing.

Surface Hardening._summary: Stainless steel has limited surface hardening capabilities. Carbon steel and low-alloy steel are hardened through martensitic transformation, but this mechanism is not very effective for stainless steel due to its low carbon content. Austenitic stainless steel can be surface hardened through nitriding, but the hardened layer is thin and hard, while the core remains soft, resulting in limited load-bearing capacity and reduced corrosion resistance. Other proprietary processes have not yet been commercialized in Australia. The PVD (Physical Vapor Deposition) process can deposit thin, hard coatings such as titanium nitride (TiN), which has a golden color and is commonly used on mirror-polished panels. However, due to the soft core, its engineering applications are also limited.

HEAT TREATMENT._summary: Heat treatment of stainless steels includes annealing, hardening, stress relieving, and surface hardening.

Passivation._summary: This content describes the method of removing contamination and enhancing corrosion resistance through passivation treatment after stainless steel surfaces are contaminated by "free iron". Passivation is a chemical process that removes iron contamination caused by carbon steel tools or grinding debris and promotes the formation of a passivation layer. Depending on the chromium content and steel type, the treatment procedures include: for steels with chromium ≥ 16% (except free-machining types such as 303), use 20-50% nitric acid at room temperature to 40°C for 30-60 minutes; for steels with chromium < 16% (except 416), use the same nitric acid treatment for 60 minutes; for free-machining types (such as 303, 416, 430F), use 20-50% nitric acid plus 2-6% sodium dichromate at room temperature to 50°C for 25-40 minutes. Precautions include: if the metallic surface luster needs to be maintained, test first; thorough rinsing is required after treatment; be aware of the corrosive hazards of nitric acid. Reference standard: ASTM A380.

Pickling._summary: This article introduces the pickling process for stainless steel, used to remove high-temperature oxide scale and red rust generated by welding, heat treatment, or hot working. Pickling enhances the corrosion resistance of stainless steel. Specific pickling solution formulations and operating conditions are provided for different stainless steel grades: for all stainless steels (except free-machining steels), use 8-11% sulfuric acid at 65-80°C for 5-45 minutes; for steels with chromium content ≥16% (except free-machining steels), use 15-25% nitric acid + 1-8% hydrofluoric acid at 20-60°C for 5-30 minutes; for free-machining steels and steels with chromium content <16%, use 10-15% nitric acid + 0.5-1.5% hydrofluoric acid at 20-60°C for 5-30 minutes. The article also emphasizes pre-treatment testing before pickling, priority treatment for annealed steel, the necessity of thorough rinsing, and safe handling of acids. Additionally, the use of pickling paste is introduced, particularly for removing heat tint after welding. Finally, it notes that the optimal approach is to avoid oxide scale formation altogether, such as by using vacuum or controlled atmosphere heat treatment.

Grinding and Polishing._summary: Stainless steel can be ground, polished, and buffed, but techniques must be adjusted to avoid surface overheating, which can cause oxidation or sensitization. Using lower speeds and feeds, selecting appropriate lubricants and abrasive grit sizes can reduce heat buildup. Coarse abrasives may impair corrosion resistance, while fine polishing (e.g., No. 4 to No. 8) can improve the surface and enhance corrosion resistance. Surface roughness Ra exceeding 0.5 microns reduces corrosion resistance. Iron contamination must be avoided; use iron-free abrasives, and perform passivation or electropolishing if necessary.

Contamination by Carbon Steel._summary: Non-stainless ferritic materials such as carbon steel, low alloy steel, tool steel, or cast iron contacting stainless steel surfaces can cause red rust spots on the stainless steel. The source of contamination can be identified by the rust pattern: intermittent or continuous rust marks indicate scratches, while scattered spots suggest airborne dust. In the early stages of contamination, only slight scratches may be visible, with rust appearing only after wetting. Detection methods include the ferroxyl test per ASTM A380 or wetting the surface with water for 24-48 hours. There are two corrosion mechanisms: one involves contact damaging the oxide film to form a corrosion cell; the other involves corrosion of carbon steel in a humid environment, leading to oxygen depletion and changes in ion concentration. Common causes of contamination include the use of carbon steel slings, contaminated lifting equipment, dragging carbon steel over stainless steel, carbon steel welding spatter, grinding dust, and tools previously used on carbon steel.

Grade Selection for Fabrication._summary: This article introduces key considerations for selecting stainless steel grades, including machinability, corrosion resistance, weldability, and formability. For applications requiring extensive machining, free-machining grades such as 303 or 416 may be considered, but attention should be paid to their lower corrosion resistance and weldability. Improved free-machining grades, such as the Ugima series (303, 304, 316), enhance machinability while maintaining the excellent performance of standard grades. For cold forming, 302HQ is suitable for fastener manufacturing, while 301 and 304, due to their high work-hardening rates, are appropriate for spring production. When welding, low-carbon L-grade or stabilized grades such as 321 should be selected to avoid sensitization issues, and welding consumables must match the base metal. It is recommended to refer to the relevant sections of this handbook on intergranular corrosion, welding, and grade selection.

Design to Avoid Corrosion._summary: This article introduces corrosion issues to be aware of in the fabrication of stainless steel, including general corrosion, pitting, crevice corrosion, intergranular corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, galvanic corrosion, and contact corrosion. Preventive measures include designing to avoid water accumulation, promoting liquid circulation, preventing evaporative concentration, reducing stress and temperature, and recommending the use of professional stainless steel manufacturers.

Selection for Corrosion Resistance._summary: This article discusses the complexity of selecting the most cost-effective stainless steel grade for corrosive environments. Typically, referencing past service experience serves as an important guide. For uniform corrosion environments such as strong acids, recommended grade tables and iso-corrosion curves can be used for comparison and selection, but it is important to note that minor differences in the environment (e.g., chlorides) can significantly affect the corrosion rate. Localized corrosion (such as pitting and crevice corrosion) is a common mechanism, influenced by chlorides and high temperatures. Its resistance is measured by the Pitting Resistance Equivalent (PRE), calculated as PRE = %Cr + 3.3%Mo + 16%N (with 0.5%W added when tungsten is present). Grades with high chromium, molybdenum, and nitrogen content (such as 316, 2205 duplex stainless steel, super austenitic, and super duplex stainless steels) exhibit stronger corrosion resistance. Additionally, common austenitic steels (e.g., 304, 316) are prone to stress corrosion cracking (SCC) in environments containing chlorides at temperatures above 60°C, while ferritic steels are almost immune, and duplex steels are highly resistant to SCC. Therefore, the appropriate grade should be selected based on the specific environment.
